content: Zinc deficiency is a major public health issue in lowand middle-income countries. Zinc plays a critical role in the development and migration of neurons, as well as in the formation of neuronal synapses. A deficiency in zinc can disrupt the formation of neural pathways and impair neurotransmission, which may negatively impact behavior (such as attention, activity levels, engagement, and temperament) and developmental milestones (including gross and fine motor skills and social skills). Providing zinc supplementation to infants and children at high risk of zinc deficiency has been proposed as a potential strategy to enhance their mental and motor development. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of zinc supplementation, compared to a placebo, on psychomotor development and cognitive function in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, LILACS, EMBASE, and CENTRAL, between December 2011 and January 2012. Additional searches were performed in Dissertation Abstracts International and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized or quasi-randomized placebo-controlled trials that involved synthetic zinc supplementation in infants or children under the age of five. Two reviewers independently screened the search results, selected eligible studies, assessed the risk of bias in the studies, and extracted relevant data. A total of 13 trials were included in the review. Eight of these studies, involving 2134 participants, provided data on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID). The data were pooled in a meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of zinc supplementation on development, as measured by the Mental Development Index (MDI) and the Psychomotor Development Index (PDI). The results showed no significant effect of zinc supplementation on mental or psychomotor development. The mean difference in MDI scores between the zinc supplementation and placebo groups was -0.50 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -2.06 to 1.06; P = 0.53; I² = 70%). Similarly, the mean difference in PDI scores between the two groups was 1.54 (95% CI: -2.26 to 5.34; P = 0.43; I² = 93%). While most studies were assessed as having a low or unclear risk of bias, there was significant heterogeneity in the results, which could not be adequately explained by subgroup analyses. The overall quality of the evidence was rated as moderate. Two trials included in the review provided data on the attainment of motor milestones. These studies found no significant difference in the time required to achieve motor milestones between the zinc supplementation group and the placebo group. None of the included studies reported data on cognitive scores, intelligence quotient (IQ), or adverse effects associated with zinc supplementation. In conclusion, there is no compelling evidence to suggest that zinc supplementation in infants or children leads to improvements in motor or mental development.
